Structures

Why wild-looking structures are safe — and why some normal-looking ones weren't.

Safety lives in how the forces flow, not in how the shape looks. A box is a habit, not a law of physics — some of the strongest structures ever built look impossible precisely because their shape IS the engineering.

THE THREE LAYERS

Read any building this way

Layer 1 · What it is

A road for forces

Every load a building ever meets — its own weight, people, snow, wind, a quake — has to travel through the structure and into the ground. That route is the load path. A structure is safe when every force has a complete, strong road home, and dangerous when a force reaches a dead end.

Layer 2 · What it means

Materials have strong directions

Stone and concrete are mighty when squeezed (compression) and weak when pulled apart (tension). Steel is the opposite star: strongest pulled in pure tension. Great structures are shapes that hand each force to the material in the direction that material is strong. Wild shapes are usually doing exactly that.

Layer 3 · What it could mean for you

You can learn to see it

Once you can follow a load path with your eyes, buildings stop being mysterious. You can stand under a shell roof a few centimetres thick and know why it holds — and you can look at a plain, normal box and ask the only question that matters: where do the forces go?

THE SHELF

Documented: shapes that look wrong and aren't

Each of these is documented fact — built, standing, and studied. The fact and its why are printed at the same size, because a fact without its why is only half a fact.

Documented · standing for millennia

The Arch

A curve that turns a downward load into a sideways squeeze. Roman aqueducts, stone bridges, and cathedral vaults have carried real weight on this shape for thousands of years — built from stone, a material that crumbles when pulled but is enormously strong when squeezed.

Why it works: the curve hands the load along itself as pure compression, stone's strong direction, and delivers it into the supports at each end. The supports must resist the outward push — that sideways thrust is the arch's one honest demand, and every real arch answers it with mass, buttresses, or buried abutments.

Documented · Gaudí, Barcelona

The Catenary

Hang a chain from two points and it settles into a curve called a catenary — the shape of pure tension, found by gravity itself. Flip that curve upside down and you get the perfect arch: a shape that carries its load in pure compression. Antoni Gaudí designed with hanging-chain models, weights and string, letting gravity draw his buildings.

Why it works: the Sagrada Família's wild forest of tilted, branching columns looks like sculpture and is actually a map — each column leans along the exact line its load travels, so the force goes straight down the stone in compression instead of bending it. The tilt is not decoration. The tilt is the load path, made visible.

Documented · Candela, Mexico

Thin Shells — the Saddle Roof

Félix Candela roofed restaurants, churches, and markets across Mexico with concrete shells only a few centimetres thick — some spanning more than 30 metres — using a saddle shape called a hyperbolic paraboloid: a surface that curves up in one direction and down in the other at the same time.

Why it works: the double curve makes the surface itself carry the load, the way a curved eggshell resists a squeeze that would crack a flat sheet. A flat concrete slab of the same few centimetres would fail under its own weight. The wild saddle is not thinner despite being safe — it is safe because of its shape. Bonus the builders loved: the saddle is made entirely of straight lines, so it can be formed with straight wooden boards.

Documented · Buckminster Fuller

The Geodesic Dome

Buckminster Fuller's dome is a sphere built from nothing but triangles — the shape used for radar domes, exhibition halls, and the famous dome at Expo 67 in Montreal. It encloses the most space with the least material of any structure on this page.

Why it works: a triangle is the one shape that cannot change shape without changing the length of a side — pin three bars into a triangle and it is locked; pin four into a square and it flops. A dome of triangles therefore spreads any load — a gust, a snow drift, a push at one point — out across the whole skin instead of letting it concentrate. No single strut carries the building; the whole surface shares every force.

Documented · Fuller & Snelson

Tensegrity

A tensegrity structure is held up by a continuous web of cables in tension, with solid struts that touch nothing — each strut floats, held in place only by the cables pulling on its ends. Kenneth Snelson built the first ones as sculpture; the principle now appears in towers, bridges, and deployable space structures.

Why it works: it looks like it should collapse, and it is remarkably hard to knock down. Push on it anywhere and the whole cable web re-shares the force — there is no single load path to break, because the load has hundreds of paths. Cut one cable and the web sags and rebalances; the structure is soft the way a net is soft, and strong the way a net is strong.

Documented · the longest spans on Earth

Suspension & Cable-Stayed Bridges

The longest bridges ever built are mostly air. The deck — the part carrying cars and trains — simply hangs: from vertical hangers, from a great sagging main cable, over the towers, and down into anchorages in the ground. Cable-stayed bridges fan their cables straight from tower to deck, like a harp.

Why it works: every cable in the system works in pure tension — steel's strongest mode, the direction in which a steel cable is nearly all strength and no waste. The deck's weight pulls down; the cables turn that pull into tension; the towers take the result as compression down into their foundations. A span that looks like a drawing of a bridge, barely there, out-carries any solid beam that could ever be built across the same water.

Tap to open — the deeper why: bending is the enemy

Nearly every shape on this shelf exists to escape one thing: bending. When a flat beam carries a load, its top squeezes and its bottom stretches — only the outer fibres work at full strength while the middle loafs, and the stretched bottom is exactly where concrete is weakest. That is why flat spans need so much material.

Curves fix this. An arch, a shell, a dome, a hanging cable — each one arranges for forces to travel along the material instead of across it, so the whole cross-section works, in the direction the material is strong. Engineers call shapes that do this form-active: the form itself is the structure. When a building looks impossibly thin or strange, the first question is never "why so weird?" — it is "what bending did this shape just refuse to do?"

FULL SIZE · NO SMALL PRINT

The honest counter-shelf

Wild shape is not automatically safe.

The safety is never in the weirdness. It is in two unglamorous things: the load path being right, and the math being checked — by engineers, against real loads, with real material strengths and margins for the day everything goes wrong at once.

Plenty of ordinary-looking buildings have failed. The Hyatt Regency walkway collapse in Kansas City (1981) happened in a plain, normal-looking hotel atrium — a small change to how the walkways were hung doubled the load on a connection, and the load path quietly stopped being the one that was designed. The Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940) looked like every other suspension bridge and tore itself apart in wind its design had not reckoned with. Both looked completely normal. Normal is not a safety feature.

And the reverse holds too: a wild shape with a wrong load path, unchecked math, or substituted materials is a sculpture waiting for weather. The shape earns nothing by itself.

Judge a structure by its load paths and its engineering — never by whether its shape looks normal.

THE HOUSE LAYER

What we would add

Design — ours, not documented factOpen how — we don't know how yet

The absorption field, for buildings

The vehicle sheets in this family — the Suit, the Ship, Cars, Bikes — are built around one idea: a field around the craft that absorbs crash energy before the structure ever has to. This sheet asks the same question of a building: what would a structure gain if earthquake and impact energy were absorbed by the building's field the way those blueprints absorb a crash?

A quake is a load like any other — it arrives at the base and hunts for a path. Today's honest answers are base isolators, dampers, and shapes that flex instead of fighting. A field that drank the shake before it entered the load path would change what a structure even has to be. How that field would work is an open how — printed here as a design question, not a claim. The documented shelf above is what stands today; this is the door we are looking at.

STANDING LAWS

Standing Laws of This Design

Three laws govern every sheet in this family, this one included. They are printed here at full size, the same as anywhere else — no small print, nothing buried.

Law 1 · The Three Modes

Spread, align, or weave — say which, and why

The Three Modes (set down November 21, 2026 · CC BY-SA 4.0). Golden — spread, never align: each new element into the biggest gap, at the golden angle 137.5077641°. Platinum — align exactly, equal, 1:1, where alignment is the function. Diamond — align locally, spread globally: the weave. Spec law: every spec involving distribution, proportion, spacing, or flow states which mode it runs and why — governed by use it when it works — don't force it.

Platinum, here: foundations, columns, and bracing aligned exactly on the load path — a column off the line is a failure, not a variation. Golden, here: redundancy and load spread — many paths, so no single member carries everything; force distributed across the frame the way a spreading root system or a fan distributes it, never concentrated in one aligned line. Diamond, here: the braced frame as a whole — members aligned exactly at their joints locally, while the bracing pattern spreads forces globally through the whole structure.

And the refusal, printed plainly: where no mode fits, none is forced. Gravity does not take a mode; a load is a load.

The full treatment lives on the Super Suit sheet as System 9 and on Sheet № 0 §14.

Law 2 · The Adaptation Clause

Adapt and overcome — learn your lessons and grow

Every build takes in new knowledge and gets better. Today's version is the floor, not the ceiling. Improvements are fitted in when verified better — never forced, and never a from-scratch rebuild.

Buildings and codes genuinely work this way: every code revision is a lesson somebody paid for, written down so the next structure stands better. This sheet is no different — when a better answer is verified, it goes in, and the record of what changed stays on the record.

Law 3 · Earned Access

With great power comes great responsibility

Access to powerful things is earned — proven by actions, never entitled, never handed out — and it can be taken away when actions prove unworthiness. The gate is not a problem with the design. It is a must.

The Resources Clause: knowing how a thing is made is great, but inert by itself — you have to have access to the resources to make it. Earned access means access to the resources, not just a permission slip.

Applied honestly to structures: the right to raise, alter, or sign off on structures other people stand under is earned and kept through demonstrated competence — engineering licensure, inspection, a track record of work that stands — and it can be lost the same way it was earned: by actions.

ACT

Standing under anything, ask three things

Ask 1

Where do the forces go?

Trace the road with your eyes: roof to walls or columns, columns to foundation, foundation to ground. A curve, a cable, a triangle — each is a sentence in that road's story. If you can't find the road, that's information too.

Ask 2

Is each force in a strong direction?

Stone and concrete want squeezing. Steel cables want pulling. Wood and steel beams bend — and bending is where the material bill comes due. A shape that respects its materials' strong directions is engineering; one that fights them is a debt.

Ask 3

Who checked the math?

The real safety certificate is never the silhouette. It is licensed engineers, reviewed calculations, inspected construction, and margins for the worst day. Ask for those, and the wildest roof in the world can earn your trust. Without them, the plainest box hasn't.
